name: Aqaba
title: Aqaba Thickness Gauging | Ship UTM at Jordan's Red Sea Port
description: Ship thickness measurement in Aqaba for phosphate and potash bulk carriers, tankers and LNG carriers: hull structure gauging and renewal survey UTM.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement and Hull Gauging in Aqaba, Jordan
intro: Aqaba is Jordan's only seaport, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, and almost everything the country moves by sea passes through it: phosphate and potash exports, grain and fuel imports, containers, vehicles and LNG. When a bulk carrier, tanker or container ship calling at Aqaba needs gauging, a team is mobilised from India to work alongside the terminals or from a launch, around the ship's cargo programme.

highlights.p: Bulk carriers loading Jordanian phosphate, potash and fertilisers at Aqaba's industrial terminals carry cargoes that are abrasive, corrosive when damp, or both. Hold frames, brackets and tank tops on these ships repay regular gauging.

highlights.h: One port for a whole country
highlights.p: As Jordan's only port, Aqaba concentrates grain, fuel, container, vehicle and LNG traffic on one stretch of coast. A single mobilisation can attend several ship types calling within the same few days.

Ships from the Mediterranean reach Aqaba through Suez without passing the Bab el-Mandeb; ships from Asia and the Gulf must transit the southern Red Sea. Attendance planning follows the ship's actual route and the owner's security guidance.

port.h: Aqaba: Jordan's port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba
p: Aqaba's terminals are spread along the Jordanian shore of the Gulf of Aqaba, from the city south towards the Saudi border. They include Aqaba Container Terminal, berths for vehicles, general cargo and project shipments, grain berths for the country's wheat and barley imports, an oil terminal for crude and product imports, an LNG import terminal using a floating storage and regasification unit, a passenger terminal for ferry services to Egypt, and the industrial terminals at the southern end where phosphate, potash and fertilisers are loaded for export. The whole port sits within the Aqaba Special Economic Zone.

The Gulf of Aqaba is a deep, narrow arm of the Red Sea entered through the Strait of Tiran, and its head is shared by four countries, with Eilat, Taba and the Saudi coast all close by. Ships reach Aqaba either from the north, through the Suez Canal and around the Sinai peninsula, or from the south, up the length of the Red Sea. Because the port serves an entire country's sea trade, its calls are dominated by cargo-driven stays: bulk carriers loading mineral exports, grain carriers discharging, and tankers and LNG carriers delivering energy imports, each with a defined berth window set by the terminal.

Gauging demand at Aqaba follows those cargoes. Potash and phosphate are hard on holds: potash is a chloride salt that turns aggressive when damp, phosphate rock is abrasive, many fertilisers are corrosive in the presence of moisture, and grab work adds mechanical damage on top. Ships on regular mineral export runs therefore build up hold wastage that has to be measured at intermediate and renewal surveys. Tankers delivering fuel and crude face the vetting and CAP questions every older tanker meets, and container and ro-ro ships on Red Sea services carry the warm-water ballast tank corrosion common to the region.

Gauging at Aqaba is done afloat, and the industrial terminals are where most of the hull work concentrates. A bulk carrier arriving in ballast to load phosphate or potash has empty holds before loading starts, and that is the moment to measure frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank tops; once loading begins, attention turns to the ballast tanks, deck plating and hatch covers. The terminals run their own safety and dust-control rules, and access is arranged through the agent and the terminal operator before the team arrives at the berth.

Elsewhere in the port, the container terminal and the general cargo and ro-ro berths allow deck, coaming, vehicle deck and accessible tank gauging during cargo calls, and the oil and LNG terminals allow deck and ballast work under their permit systems. Ships waiting for a berth can be boarded by launch where the harbour authority allows it. Where a ship's next docking is at Suez or in the Gulf, the Aqaba readings travel with it, so the yard has measured wastage before the ship arrives and the docking period can be planned from figures rather than from the previous survey alone.
list: Aqaba industrial terminals — phosphate, potash and fertiliser loading berths near the Saudi border; empty-hold gauging of frames, hopper plating and tank tops before loading.
Aqaba Container Terminal — container calls on Red Sea and international services; deck, hatch coaming, scrubber piping and accessible tank gauging alongside.
Grain and general cargo berths — wheat and barley imports and project cargo; hold gauging after discharge and deck work during cargo operations.
Oil and LNG terminals — crude, product and LNG imports; deck, ballast tank and deck-piping gauging under the terminals' permit systems.
Ro-ro and ferry berths — vehicle imports and passenger services to Egypt; vehicle deck, ramp and tank gauging between calls.

context.h: Jordanian port state control, the economic zone and the Red Sea route
p: Port state control at Aqaba is carried out by Jordan's maritime authority under the Mediterranean MoU. The port lies inside the Aqaba Special Economic Zone, which has its own customs and administrative arrangements, so passes, equipment clearance and terminal access all run through the ship's agent. In the Gulf of Aqaba only the global 0.50% sulphur cap applies, but ships on services that continue through Suez enter the Mediterranean ECA as they leave the canal at Port Said, which keeps scrubber piping condition on the agenda for container lines calling here.

Ships coming from the Mediterranean reach Aqaba through Suez and the Strait of Tiran without passing the Bab el-Mandeb, while ships from Asia, the Gulf and East Africa must transit the southern Red Sea, an area of attacks on merchant shipping since late 2023. That distinction affects which services call and how owners route them, and attendance at Aqaba is planned within each owner's security guidance. For Jordanian importers and mineral exporters, Aqaba remains the country's only sea gateway, so its cargo flows keep bringing bulk carriers, tankers and LNG carriers to its berths.

jobs.p: Aqaba's scenarios are set by its cargoes: mineral exports, grain and fuel imports, LNG deliveries, and container and vehicle traffic. Each job below fits the berth window those cargoes create, and the scope is drawn up from the ship's survey position, the terminal's access rules and the visa timing for a team travelling from India. Where several ships call in the same week, one mobilisation can cover them.
list: Potash carrier hold gauging before loading at the industrial terminals, measuring frames, lower brackets and tank tops on a handysize bulk carrier ahead of its renewal survey.
Phosphate bulk carrier gauging after a long run of export voyages, re-measuring hopper plating and any substantial-corrosion areas noted at the previous intermediate survey.
Measuring deck plating and ballast tanks on a product tanker as it discharges at the oil terminal, for an operator preparing the ship for vetting or a CAP survey.
Ballast tank and vehicle deck gauging on a passenger and vehicle ferry serving Egypt, ahead of its annual survey, with the work fitted between crossings.
Overboard and wash-water line readings on a scrubber-fitted container ship alongside at Aqaba Container Terminal, taken before its northbound passage to Suez and the Mediterranean ECA.

logistics: King Hussein International Airport in Aqaba is the nearest arrival point, and Queen Alia International Airport near Amman offers wider connections with a road transfer south to the coast. The port terminals are ISPS-controlled and sit inside the special economic zone, so the ship's agent sorts out personal passes and an equipment clearance, using passport details supplied in advance, and books a launch for any boarding away from the berth. Each technician's Jordanian visa is secured before departure from India, so knowing the ETA or loading window early is what fixes the mobilisation date.
vessels: Bulk carriers in the phosphate and potash trades

faqs.q: When should holds be gauged on a potash or phosphate carrier at Aqaba?
faqs.a: Before loading starts, when the ship has arrived in ballast with empty holds. That gives clear access to frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank tops before the cargo goes in. If the holds need cleaning first, the chief officer, the terminal and the team work out an order in which gauging follows cleaning and hold inspection without delaying the loading slot.

faqs.q: Do you offer ship inspection in Jordan outside Aqaba?
faqs.a: Aqaba is Jordan's only seaport, so ship work in Jordan means Aqaba. The same mobilisation can, however, be extended to the Egyptian ports at the southern end of the Suez Canal, to Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports, or to Port Said, depending on visas and on where the fleet's other ships are calling.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a tanker or LNG carrier at Aqaba?
faqs.a: Yes, for deck and ballast tank work under the terminal's permit system. Cargo tanks on a tanker, and the cargo containment on an LNG carrier, are out of reach during a cargo call, so the useful scope is the deck plate, the deck pipe runs, the ballast tanks and any accessible void spaces, with equipment and work zones cleared with the terminal first.

faqs.q: What paperwork does thickness measurement in Jordan need?
faqs.a: A visa for each technician travelling from India, port passes arranged through the ship's agent, and clearance for the gauging equipment to enter the special economic zone and the terminal. We start these as soon as the ship's ETA or loading window is known, and confirm with the agent which terminal rules and inductions apply.
